content:
Reports indicate that code discovered in the camera app of the latest iOS 27 beta appears to foreshadow several upcoming professional-grade photo and video features.

Although the built-in camera app has gradually incorporated more features over the years, these discoveries are still somewhat unexpected, given that the app is primarily designed for casual, point-and-shoot use……

Apple has always tried to strike a balance between the two—on one hand, designing the camera app to be extremely easy to operate for quick snapshots; on the other hand, providing a degree of creative control for users who wish to use it as a serious photography tool. However, although this app has gradually evolved, most photo and video enthusiasts still tend to use third-party apps.

If these findings prove accurate, some powerful features typically exclusive to high-end cameras could fundamentally change the current landscape. Developer pdfu said they found code supporting four major features, though none of them have been enabled in the current beta version.

Exposure Aids

Judging exposure by the naked eye is usually unreliable, and it becomes even more difficult to view the iPhone screen under harsh sunlight. Most professional cameras support a histogram feature that accurately displays the exposure status; video editing software typically uses a waveform monitor as an alternative. According to pdfu, they found code related to both features in the beta version.

Focus Peaking

How much of a scene—from the nearest foreground to the farthest background—remains sharp and in focus is affected by several factors, but under certain shooting conditions, only parts of the image stay sharp. Likewise, judging by sight which areas are in focus and which are not is not entirely reliable, so professional-grade cameras have specifically adopted a method called focus peaking.

When this feature is enabled, an overlay can be activated to mark the areas that are in focus, typically in red—though the example on the left uses yellow.

Overexposure (Highlight Clipping) Warning

The most serious risk of exposure error is overexposure. Generally speaking, if the shadows are underexposed, it can usually be rescued in post-processing—unless the situation is extremely severe, shadows will rarely go completely black (i.e., an RGB value of zero). Overexposure is far more serious, because highlights can easily become completely "clipped"—that is, exceeding an RGB value of 255—and no amount of post-processing can recover them.

Many professional cameras use a feature called zebra stripes, which uses red diagonal lines to mark completely clipped areas. Some cameras even allow users to manually set the threshold for this warning, so you can be alerted when approaching overexposure (e.g., at 90%) rather than waiting until actual clipping occurs.

This feature is also shown on the right side of the image above.

Manual Focus

Currently, although the camera app can lock focus on a subject in the frame, it must also lock the exposure at that point via AE/AF Lock (Auto Exposure/Auto Focus) at the same time.

Reports indicate that Apple has been testing a true manual focus feature that can be operated via a slider within the camera app. According to pdfu, this feature may be limited to one or more upcoming new iPhone models.

Other Features

In addition to the professional features, it is also reported that an option is being added to take a continuous series of timed selfies. People who want to take group photos often want to take a few extra shots; this feature would let everyone place the phone on a tripod or other flat surface, then take a continuous series of photos, and pick one that everyone is happy with.

Finally, there are also indications that a new image processing method will be adopted to accommodate a variable aperture design expected to appear on the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac's Take

None of the features mentioned above have been enabled in any iOS 27 beta version so far. I would personally be quite surprised if Apple put these features in the built-in camera app rather than restricting them to Final Cut Camera—but the report does appear to be quite credible.

What are your thoughts on this report? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
